Among the small pelagic clupeiform fishes of the tropical Indo-Pacific, the long-jawed anchovy Stolephorus commersonnii attains a maximum total length of 14.5 cm [Li = 14.5 cm], a modest size that positions it among the smaller members of the family Engraulidae. Field surveys conducted across coastal waters of the western Indian Ocean indicate that this species rarely exceeds this benchmark, with most captured individuals measuring between 10 and 13 cm. The ultimate total length is consistent with the energetic constraints imposed by a fast-paced life history, wherein early maturation and elevated reproductive output are prioritized over extended somatic growth. Comparative morphometric data from related species such as Stolephorus indicus and Stolephorus heterolobus suggest that this ceiling in body size may be linked to the thermal regimes of the warm, shallow inshore habitats the long-jawed anchovy frequents. Juvenile specimens commonly recruit to estuarine nurseries before gradually moving toward more open waters as they approach their adult dimensions. The relatively small asymptotic length is also reflected in the species' body mass relationships, with the ultimate wet weight predicted from length-weight regressions to be approximately 25.3 grams [Wwi = approximately 25.3 grams], a value that underscores the slender, streamlined morphology typical of obligate planktivores.

Reproductive maturation in Stolephorus commersonnii occurs at a total body length of 7.2 cm [Lp = 7.2 cm], a threshold that is reached several months after settlement into juvenile habitats. Histological examinations of gonadal tissue confirm that individuals at this length exhibit active gametogenesis, with both spermatogenesis and vitellogenesis underway. The length at puberty is notably small relative to the ultimate size of the species, representing about half of the maximum recorded total length — a pattern indicative of early reproductive investment commonly observed in short-lived, iteroparous small pelagics. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is estimated to be 2.73 grams [Wwp = 2.73 grams], derived from the species-specific length-weight conversion. This body composition marks the transition from immature sub-adults to reproductively viable individuals capable of contributing to the next generation. Interestingly, some variation in size at maturity has been noted across different populations, with individuals from cooler upwelling zones tending to reach puberty at slightly larger dimensions than those from warmer, more stable coastal waters. Nonetheless, the 7.2 cm benchmark serves as a reliable reference for the onset of reproductive capacity in this species.

Under the prevailing thermal conditions of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C], typical of the tropical surface waters this anchovy inhabits, newly hatched larvae emerge from their spherical, transparent eggs after a brief embryonic period of approximately 3 days [ab = approximately 3 days]. The eggs themselves have a diameter of about 0.8 mm, from which the wet weight at birth has been calculated at 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams], reflecting the diminutive size of the yolk-sac larva at the moment of hatching. At this stage, the prolarva remains entirely dependent on endogenous yolk reserves, its mouth not yet fully formed for exogenous feeding. Within the same thermal regime, the maximum recorded longevity for the species reaches 365 days [am = 365 days], indicating a naturally short lifespan typical of many small, rapidly maturing clupeiforms at a temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. A full year thus represents the complete generational turnover period in this fish, with most individuals spawning in their first and only breeding season before senescent decline. This compressed lifespan places substantial selective pressure on early reproductive output, driving the elevated fecundity observed in mature females.

During spawning events at 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C], gravid females release multiple batches of pelagic eggs over the course of a single reproductive season. Observations of captive individuals indicate that each female can produce approximately 10,033 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 10,033 eggs per spawning event], and the spawning frequency is typically once per year [F_R_i = spawning frequency is typically once per year]. This annual reproductive output, when contextualized by the species' body size, represents a considerable investment relative to somatic mass. The spawning frequency is strongly seasonal rather than continuous, with females maintaining gravid condition primarily during the warm monsoon-driven productivity peaks. The elevated fecundity is typical of r-selected strategies and helps offset the high natural mortality rates that planktonic eggs and early larval stages experience in the pelagic environment. Predation by gelatinous zooplankton, larval competition, and stochastic oceanographic events collectively ensure that only a tiny fraction of the eggs released survive to recruitment, reinforcing the need for high per-event fecundity to maintain population stability.

The combination of early maturation, short lifespan, and prolific egg output places Stolephorus commersonnii squarely within the fast end of the life-history continuum for marine teleosts. Individuals transition from yolk-dependent prolarvae to actively feeding, free-swimming larvae within the first week post-hatching, undergoing rapid fin ray ossification and scale formation during the first several weeks. Larval metamorphosis and the pelagic-benthic transition to coastal juvenile habitats typically occur within the first month, after which the growing juvenile experiences a period of rapid mass increase leading up to the 7.2 cm [Lp = 7.2 cm] puberty threshold. By the time the fish reaches the ultimate length of 14.5 cm [Li = 14.5 cm], which corresponds to the 25.3 gram [Wwi = 25.3 gram] adult mass, it has already expended considerable energetic resources on repeated spawning bouts. The species' position within coastal food webs is pivotal, linking primary and secondary planktonic production to higher-level piscivores. Population dynamics are heavily influenced by seasonal monsoon-driven productivity cycles, which drive prey availability and, consequently, reproductive timing.
